name: Carbon dioxide freckle removal (CO2 snow)

card.summary: An early-20th-century dermatology technique that touched frozen carbon dioxide snow to freckles to lighten them for a clearer complexion.
card.note: Freezing skin can cause pigment changes, especially in darker skin tones.

quick.overview:
Carbon dioxide snow is the slush or pressed solid form of CO2 (dry ice). Historical accounts describe dermatologists applying it briefly to skin spots, including freckles, to remove or fade them for an evenly toned face.

It is a forerunner of modern cryotherapy, which uses liquid nitrogen for warts, moles, skin tags and sun spots. Practitioners of the era protected the eyes during treatment of facial skin.
quick.how: It was a clinic procedure performed by physicians, not a home routine; modern equivalents are done by dermatologists.
quick.risks: Freezing damages skin cells, and cryotherapy carries a high risk of lightening (hypopigmentation) in people with darker skin [1]. Blistering and scarring are possible with freezing treatments.

lead: Carbon dioxide snow freckle removal refers to a historical cosmetic-dermatology practice in which solid carbon dioxide was applied to freckles to destroy or fade the pigmented skin. Accounts place it in the 1930s, when patients reportedly wore eye protection during facial treatment.

It belongs to the family of cryotherapy, in which cold damages targeted tissue; modern skin cryosurgery typically uses liquid nitrogen for lesions such as warts, moles, skin tags and solar keratoses, and tissue damage depends on how cold and how fast the skin is cooled [1].

chain: Lighter, more even skin as it heals
angle.text: The goal was fewer or paler freckles on the face. Modern dermatology uses other methods for pigmented spots.

paras: Freezing agents act by forming ice inside cells, with damage depending on temperature and cooling speed [1].
Skin cryosurgery carries a high risk of hypopigmentation in dark-skinned individuals, which matters for any freezing of pigmented skin [1].
